5.Standing under Article III is a jurisdictional limitation on the power of federal courts to adjudicate a dispute. See p. 719, Note 3, supra. In
TRANSUNION LLC v. RAMIREZ, 594 U.S. ___, 141 S.Ct. 2190, 210 L.Ed.2d 568 (2021), the Supreme Court held that each member of a class
seeking damages must satisfy Article III’s standing requirement. The class consisted of 8,185 consumers who sued TransUnion, a consumer credit
reporting company, in federal court for preparing credit reports with inaccurate personal information. The complaint alleged that TransUnion had
added a misleading notice that the class members were on the list of “specially designated nationals” compiled by the United States Treasury
Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control. That list included terrorists, drug traffickers, and others deemed to pose a threat to national security.
The class brought claims under state law and under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), which regulates entities that provide consumer credit reports.
The FCRA includes a cause of action for consumers to recover actual damages, statutory damages, and punitive damages against “[a]ny person who
willfully fails to comply” with the statutory requirements. 15 U.S.C. § 1681n(a). The complaint asserted that TransUnion had violated the FCRA by
failing to use reasonable procedures to ensure the accuracy of the class members’ credit reports and by failing to provide class members with a
summary of rights under the statute and appropriate disclosures about their credit reports.
The district court certified the class over TransUnion’s objections. Before trial, the parties stipulated that TransUnion had disseminated the credit
reports of only 1,853 members of the class to potential creditors during the relevant time period. The jury awarded statutory and punitive damages
totaling $60 million. A divided panel of the Ninth Circuit reduced the punitive award but held that all members of the class had Article III standing to
recover damages. The court also concluded that the class representative’s claims were typical of the class’s claims for purposes of Rule 23.
The Supreme Court reversed as to standing and remanded for the Ninth Circuit to reconsider whether class certification was appropriate. Justice
Kavanaugh, joined by four justices, concluded that only the class members whose credit reports had been disseminated to potential creditors
“demonstrated concrete reputational harm” sufficient to establish Article III standing to sue in federal court. By contrast, the remaining 6,332 class
members whose credit files had not been provided to third parties during the relevant time period had not suffered a concrete harm and thus lacked
Article III standing. The majority explained:
As the party invoking federal jurisdiction, the plaintiffs bear the burden of demonstrating that they have standing. Every class member must
